metadata.title: Orthopedic Surgery & Musculoskeletal Disorders
metadata.description: Multiple-choice questions organized by topics and chapters.

questions.question: During hip examination, when performing the Thomas test, the patient's thigh lifts off the table as the opposite hip is flexed. What is the most likely finding?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Patient lies supine while the contralateral hip is maximally flexed to flatten the lumbar lordosis. The ipsilateral (test) thigh involuntarily lifts off the examination couch, indicating an inability to achieve neutral hip extension.

The Thomas test is the classic clinical test used to detect fixed flexion contracture (tightness) of the hip, primarily involving the iliopsoas muscle complex. The patient is placed supine, and the examiner's hand is placed under the lumbar spine. The contralateral uninvolved hip is flexed until the lumbar lordosis is completely flattened. If the ipsilateral (tested) thigh lifts off the table or fails to remain flat, a positive test indicates fixed hip flexion deformity caused by tightness or contracture of the primary hip flexor—the iliopsoas.

High-yield takeaway: In a positive Thomas test, excessive lumbar lordosis is eliminated by flexing the opposite hip; if the test limb rises off the table, it confirms fixed flexion deformity of the hip (iliopsoas contracture).

Exam trap: Patients often compensate for an iliopsoas flexion contracture by increasing their lumbar lordosis while standing or lying down, masking the deformity unless the pelvis is properly locked flat.

optionExplanations.A: Tensor fascia lata (TFL) and iliotibial band tightness are assessed primarily with the Ober test, where the hip is abducted and extended in the lateral decubitus position.
optionExplanations.B: Gluteus medius weakness is evaluated using the Trendelenburg test (observing pelvic drop during single-leg stance), not the Thomas test.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The Thomas test is the classic clinical test used to detect fixed flexion contracture (tightness) of the hip, primarily involving the iliopsoas muscle complex.
optionExplanations.D: Gluteus maximus is the primary hip extensor; weakness would impair hip extension and rising from a seated position, rather than causing a flexion contracture.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that lifting of the test thigh off the examination table during the Thomas test confirms fixed hip flexion contracture secondary to iliopsoas tightness.

questions.question: A football player came with a heel injury, and surgery shows the following finding. Which of the following is the best test to apply in this case?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Intraoperative surgical photograph demonstrating an open posterior ankle exploration with a complete transverse rupture and fraying of the Achilles (calcaneal) tendon fibers ('mop-end' appearance) requiring primary surgical repair.

The surgical finding demonstrates an acute complete rupture of the Achilles tendon (tendo calcaneus). The definitive clinical diagnostic maneuver is the Thompson test (Simmonds-Thompson test). With the patient prone and the feet hanging over the edge of the table (or kneeling on a chair), the examiner squeezes the calf (gastrocnemius-soleus complex). In a normal tendon, this causes passive ankle plantarflexion. In a complete Achilles tendon rupture, squeezing the calf produces no plantarflexion (positive test).

High-yield takeaway: The Thompson (calf squeeze) test is nearly 100% sensitive for complete Achilles tendon rupture. Absence of passive ankle plantarflexion upon calf compression confirms tendon discontinuity.

Exam trap: Do not assume an intact Achilles tendon just because the patient can weakly plantarflex while non-weight bearing; accessory flexors (tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus) can still produce weak non-weight-bearing plantarflexion.

optionExplanations.A: The Thomas test assesses fixed flexion deformity of the hip, not posterior ankle injuries.
optionExplanations.B: The anterior drawer test of the ankle evaluates the integrity of the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) following inversion ankle sprains.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The Thompson (calf-squeeze) test is the diagnostic maneuver for a complete Achilles tendon rupture: with the patient prone, squeezing the calf produces no passive plantarflexion.
optionExplanations.D: The McMurray test is used to evaluate meniscal tears of the knee.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the Thompson test (calf squeeze maneuver) as the gold-standard physical examination test for diagnosing acute complete rupture of the Achilles tendon.

questions.question: According to this image, which gait-cycle phase will be affected?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Clinical photograph of the plantar aspect of the forefoot showing multiple painful, hyperkeratotic plantar lesions (verrucae/callosities) directly overlying the metatarsal heads and distal toes.

Painful plantar lesions located over the forefoot and metatarsal heads (metatarsalgia, verrucae, or callosities) cause an antalgic gait characterized by rapid unloading of the forefoot. During the stance phase of the gait cycle, the final subphase is terminal stance / preswing, known as 'push-off' (or toe-off), where body weight rolls onto the metatarsal heads and toes. To minimize intense pain during weight transfer onto these painful plantar lesions, the patient prematurely lifts the foot, resulting in shortening of the push-off (toe-off) phase.

High-yield takeaway: Antalgic gait modifications directly correspond to the anatomical site of pain: heel pain shortens heel strike, midfoot pain shortens midstance, and forefoot/toe pain shortens terminal push-off.

Exam trap: Always differentiate between heel strike pathology (calcaneus/Achilles) and push-off pathology (metatarsals/toes/gastrosoleus).

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Painful forefoot/metatarsal-head plantar lesions make the patient unload the forefoot early, so the terminal-stance 'push-off' (toe-off) phase of gait is shortened.
optionExplanations.B: Shortening of heel strike occurs with calcaneal pathology, retrocalcaneal bursitis, or acute heel spurs/plantar fasciitis at the calcaneal origin.
optionExplanations.C: The swing phase is non-weight-bearing; painful plantar contact lesions do not lengthen the swing phase.
optionExplanations.D: Antalgic gait primarily reduces the stance time on the affected limb rather than shortening the non-weight-bearing swing phase.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand that painful forefoot plantar lesions impair weight transfer at the conclusion of stance, leading to antalgic shortening of the toes push-off phase.

questions.question: A 24-year-old male athlete presents with hip pain aggravated by running. Physical examination reveals tightness of iliopsoas with a fixed hip flexion. Which of the following clinical tests is the most appropriate to assess his condition?
questions.explanation:
In an athlete presenting with suspected iliopsoas tightness and fixed hip flexion, the Thomas test is the definitive clinical maneuver. By maximally flexing the uninvolved contralateral hip to eliminate compensatory lumbar lordosis, any inability of the affected thigh to lie flat on the examination table confirms iliopsoas shortening or flexion contracture.

High-yield takeaway: The Thomas test isolates iliopsoas contracture by locking the pelvis in posterior pelvic tilt via full contralateral hip flexion, preventing false-negative assessments due to lumbar hyperlordosis.

Exam trap: Do not confuse the Thomas test (hip flexion contracture) with the Thompson test (Achilles tendon rupture). The names sound similar but assess completely different joints.

optionExplanations.A: Thompson test evaluates Achilles tendon integrity by squeezing the calf.
optionExplanations.B: Trendelenburg test evaluates the abductor mechanism of the hip (gluteus medius and minimus) innervated by the superior gluteal nerve.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. In an athlete presenting with suspected iliopsoas tightness and fixed hip flexion, the Thomas test is the definitive clinical maneuver.
optionExplanations.D: Finkelstein test is diagnostic for de Quervain tenosynovitis of the first dorsal wrist compartment.

questions.educationalObjective: Select the Thomas test as the primary physical examination maneuver to quantify iliopsoas muscle tightness and hip flexion contractures.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct according to the photo?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Anatomical schematic illustration showing the posterior lower leg musculature (gastrocnemius, soleus), converging into the thick calcaneal (Achilles) tendon and inserting onto the posterior tuberosity of the calcaneus.

The image demonstrates the anatomy of the gastrocnemius-soleus complex inserting via the Achilles tendon onto the calcaneus. Pathology of this musculotendinous unit (specifically complete Achilles rupture) is diagnosed clinically via the Thompson test (Simmonds test). A positive Thompson test (loss of plantarflexion upon calf squeeze) confirms complete disruption of this anatomical structure.

High-yield takeaway: The Achilles tendon is the strongest and thickest tendon in the human body, formed by the conjoined aponeuroses of the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles.

Exam trap: Remember that a normal response to calf compression is passive ankle plantarflexion; a 'positive' Thompson test is abnormal and indicates tendon disruption.

optionExplanations.A: The Thomas test examines the anterior hip flexors (iliopsoas), not the posterior leg/Achilles tendon.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The image shows the gastrocnemius-soleus complex and Achilles tendon; Achilles rupture is tested with the Thompson test, which is positive when calf squeezing produces no plantarflexion.
optionExplanations.C: The Trendelenburg test evaluates gluteal abductor function at the pelvis/hip, not the ankle.

questions.educationalObjective: Correlate Achilles tendon anatomy with the Thompson calf-squeeze test for detecting tendon rupture.

questions.question: A middle-aged female presents with a 3-day history of burning pain followed by the appearance of grouped vesicular lesions over an erythematous base, distributed along a single dermatome and not crossing the midline. What is the most appropriate basis for making the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Clinical photograph of cutaneous grouped vesicles and crusted papules on an erythematous plaque sharply confined to a single thoracic dermatomal band without crossing the anatomical midline.

Herpes zoster (shingles) is caused by reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) residing in dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia. The presentation of unifocal, prodromal radicular burning pain or dysesthesia followed by a classic eruption of grouped, fluid-filled vesicles on an erythematous base confined strictly to a single dermatome (unilateral, terminating sharply at the midline) is pathognomonic. The diagnosis is clinical, based on history and physical examination alone, without requiring routine laboratory or virological confirmation.

Other options (source): Other modalities: Viral PCR, Tzanck smear, or viral culture may be used in atypical, disseminated, or immunocompromised presentations, but straightforward dermatomal shingles is definitively diagnosed on clinical grounds.

High-yield takeaway: Unilateral dermatomal pain preceding a vesicular rash that does not cross the midline is diagnostic of Herpes Zoster. Prompt initiation of oral antivirals (e.g., valacyclovir within 72 hours) reduces acute pain and postherpetic neuralgia risk.

Exam trap: Before the rash appears, the pre-eruptive neuropathic pain can mimic acute orthopedic or surgical emergencies such as cervical/lumbar radiculopathy, pleurisy, cholecystitis, or renal colic.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Classic unilateral dermatomal herpes zoster (burning prodrome, then grouped vesicles that do not cross the midline) is diagnosed clinically, from history and physical examination alone.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that classic unilateral dermatomal herpes zoster is diagnosed clinically based on history and physical examination.

questions.question: What is the MOST likely cause of the limping seen in this image?

options.A: Injury to the left superior gluteal nerve
options.B: Injury to the left inferior gluteal nerve
options.C: Injury to the left superior gluteal artery
options.D: Injury to the right superior gluteal artery

questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Posterior view photograph of a walking male patient demonstrating a compensated abductor lurch (Trendelenburg gait): when standing on the left lower extremity, the trunk excessively tilts laterally over the left hip to maintain balance because of left gluteus medius/minimus insufficiency.

The image demonstrates a patient leaning/lurching their trunk over the left weight-bearing limb during gait (compensated Trendelenburg gait). The hip abductors (gluteus medius and gluteus minimus) are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1). When the left superior gluteal nerve is injured (or left abductor muscles are impaired), the left abductor mechanism cannot stabilize the pelvis during the stance phase on the left. The patient must excessively lean the torso toward the ipsilateral (left) side to bring the center of gravity over the stance hip and prevent contralateral pelvic drop.

High-yield takeaway: In Trendelenburg sign/gait: The pathology is on the STANCE (supporting) side. If standing on the LEFT leg causes trunk lean to the left (compensated) or pelvic drop to the right (uncompensated), the lesion is in the LEFT superior gluteal nerve or left gluteus medius.

Exam trap: Always distinguish between the weak side (ipsilateral to stance and trunk lean) and the dropping side (contralateral, unsupported side). The lesion is ALWAYS on the side of the supported weight-bearing leg.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve; a left-sided injury causes the compensated Trendelenburg gait, with trunk lean over the left stance limb.
optionExplanations.B: The inferior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus maximus; injury causes a gluteus maximus lurch (backward trunk lean at heel strike to prevent forward collapse), not a lateral abductor lurch.
optionExplanations.C: Vascular injuries alone without nerve disruption do not cause isolated neurogenic abductor palsy.
optionExplanations.D: Vascular injuries alone without nerve disruption do not cause isolated neurogenic abductor palsy.
optionExplanations.E: Right developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) would cause pelvic drop when standing on the right leg, or trunk lean to the right.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify injury to the ipsilateral superior gluteal nerve as the cause of gluteus medius weakness and resulting Trendelenburg gait.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about this test ?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Schematic diagram of the Trendelenburg test viewed from behind. Figure (a) shows normal pelvic elevation when standing on one leg. Figure (b) shows standing on the left leg with the pelvis sagging downward on the unsupported right side, demonstrating a positive left Trendelenburg test.

In diagram (b), the patient is weight-bearing on the left lower limb, and the pelvis drops downward on the contralateral (right) swing side. This represents a positive Trendelenburg sign on the left. A positive test indicates failure of the left hip abductor mechanism, which can be caused by superior gluteal nerve injury, gluteus medius tears, or structural hip disorders that reduce the abductor lever arm, such as left Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH), coxa vara, or chronic hip dislocation.

High-yield takeaway: Trendelenburg sign is positive when the pelvis drops toward the unsupported (normal) side. The lesion (e.g., DDH, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, superior gluteal nerve palsy) is on the STANCE side.

Exam trap: Students often mistakenly choose the side of pelvic depression. Remember: the pelvis drops because the OPPOSITE (stance) abductors fail to contract and hold it up.

optionExplanations.A: Right-sided abductor weakness or right DDH would cause pelvic drop when the patient stands on the right leg, resulting in left hemipelvis drop.
optionExplanations.B: Right-sided abductor weakness or right DDH would cause pelvic drop when the patient stands on the right leg, resulting in left hemipelvis drop.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. In diagram (b), the patient is weight-bearing on the left lower limb, and the pelvis drops downward on the contralateral (right) swing side.

questions.educationalObjective: Deduce that contralateral pelvic sag during unilateral stance indicates an abductor mechanism defect (such as DDH) in the ipsilateral weight-bearing hip.

questions.question: A 46-year-old female came to the ER after a high-energy accident. X-ray shows a fracture in the femur shaft, and the patient was stabilized. After 8 hours, she suddenly started to complain of dyspnea and decreased level of consciousness. According to this case, which of the following is correct?

options.A: The most likely diagnosis is pulmonary embolism
options.B: DVT is suspected and Doppler ultrasound is indicated
options.C: External fixation of the fracture using appropriate approaches

questions.explanation:
This patient is developing Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES), which typically manifests 12 to 72 hours following long bone (especially femoral shaft) or pelvic fractures. In polytrauma patients or patients developing acute respiratory and neurological compromise from fat embolism, early temporary stabilization via external fixation (Damage Control Orthopedics [DCO]) minimizes further mechanical disruption of the marrow, prevents ongoing fat and cytokine embolization into the venous circulation, and allows intensive pulmonary support and resuscitation.

High-yield takeaway: Fat Embolism Syndrome Triad: Respiratory distress (hypoxemia), Neurological dysfunction (confusion, altered sensorium), and Petechial rash (conjunctival, axillary, anterior chest). Damage control external fixation prevents progressive intravasation of marrow fat.

Exam trap: Do not confuse fat embolism (onset within 24-72 hours with petechiae and confusion) with venous thromboembolism (rarely occurs within <24 hours of acute injury).

optionExplanations.A: Thromboembolic pulmonary embolism secondary to deep vein thrombosis typically takes several days to develop (peak incidence 5-10 days post-injury), unlike fat embolism which occurs within 12-72 hours of long bone trauma.
optionExplanations.B: Thromboembolic pulmonary embolism secondary to deep vein thrombosis typically takes several days to develop (peak incidence 5-10 days post-injury), unlike fat embolism which occurs within 12-72 hours of long bone trauma.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The picture is fat embolism syndrome after a femoral shaft fracture; early temporary stabilization by external fixation (damage-control orthopedics) limits further marrow embolization and is the best choice among the listed options.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the role of rapid fracture stabilization (external fixation) in managing long bone fractures complicated by or at risk for fat embolism syndrome.

questions.question: A patient came with a Gustilo type 3B fracture. He was stable with BP 130/80. Other systems were normal by labs and investigations. After starting management, his consciousness started to decrease with BP 90/50. The cause is:

options.A: Neurogenic shock during transportation in the ambulance
options.B: Hypotensive shock due to major artery injury
options.C: These symptoms were due to given IV antibiotic
options.D: The patient has a femoral nerve injury

questions.explanation:
In an open fracture (Gustilo-Anderson type 3B), emergent prophylactic intravenous antibiotics (typically a first-generation cephalosporin such as cefazolin combined with an aminoglycoside) are administered immediately. An abrupt drop in blood pressure from 130/80 to 90/50 accompanied by altered mental status shortly after initiating therapy indicates drug-induced anaphylactic (distributive) shock. Cefazolin and other beta-lactams are the leading cause of perioperative anaphylaxis, triggering IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation, systemic vasodilation, and relative hypovolemia.

High-yield takeaway: Intravenous antibiotics administered for open fractures are a frequent source of acute perioperative anaphylaxis, manifesting with rapid-onset hypotension, tachycardia, and altered mental perfusion.

Exam trap: Always re-evaluate the timing of sudden clinical deterioration relative to new medication administration before assuming ongoing occult bleeding.

optionExplanations.A: Neurogenic shock occurs with high spinal cord injury (cervical/upper thoracic) causing hypotension and bradycardia; the patient was stable in the ER.
optionExplanations.B: A major arterial injury (type 3C) would present with absent distal pulses, limb ischemia, and early hypovolemic shock prior to initial ER stabilization.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A sudden fall in blood pressure (130/80 to 90/50) with reduced consciousness shortly after starting IV antibiotics indicates drug-induced anaphylactic (distributive) shock; beta-lactams such as cefazolin are a leading cause.
optionExplanations.D: Isolated femoral nerve injury causes quadriceps motor deficit and anterior thigh sensory loss without systemic hypotension.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that acute hypotension and altered mental status occurring immediately following the start of medical management in a previously stable trauma patient points to antibiotic-induced anaphylaxis.

questions.question: A 27-year-old male was involved in a high-energy road traffic accident. On arrival, his right leg was severely deformed with an open wound, exposed bone fragments, and active bleeding. Distal pulses were weak. He was taken urgently to the operating room where an external fixator spanning the tibia was applied. What is the MOST appropriate reason for choosing external fixation in this patient?

options.B: Because external fixation is less painful than casting
options.C: Open fracture with severe soft tissue injury
options.D: Because internal fixation is contraindicated in all tibial fractures

questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Clinical photograph of a patient with a circular/ring external fixator (Ilizarov apparatus) applied to the lower leg, providing rigid skeletal stabilization across an extensive contaminated open tibial wound.

External fixation is primarily indicated for high-energy open fractures with severe soft tissue compromise (Gustilo-Anderson Grade IIIB and IIIC) and in hemodynamically unstable polytrauma patients (damage control orthopedics). Placing internal hardware (plates, intramedullary nails) into an extensive, highly contaminated open wound with stripped periosteum carries a prohibitively high risk of deep osteomyelitis, implant infection, and hardware failure. External fixator pins are placed outside the contaminated zone of injury, providing immediate skeletal stability while allowing unobstructed access for serial wound debridement and vascular or soft-tissue coverage.

High-yield takeaway: External fixation is the gold-standard temporary or definitive skeletal stabilization method in open fractures with severe soft tissue compromise, contamination, or vascular injury.

Exam trap: Do not attempt immediate definitive plate osteosynthesis through contaminated, devitalized soft tissue envelopes.

optionExplanations.A: External fixation provides relative stability and length/alignment restoration, but rarely achieves the exact rigid anatomical reduction provided by open reduction and internal plate fixation.
optionExplanations.B: External fixation is not chosen for pain management compared to casting.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. External fixation is primarily indicated for high-energy open fractures with severe soft tissue compromise (Gustilo-Anderson Grade IIIB and IIIC) and in hemodynamically unstable polytrauma patients (damage control orthopedics).
optionExplanations.D: Internal fixation (such as reamed intramedullary nailing) is actually the gold standard for closed or low-grade open tibial fractures once soft tissue envelopes allow.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify severe open soft tissue injury and high contamination risk as the primary indications for applying external skeletal fixation.

questions.question: A 27-year-old male construction worker presents 6 hours after a crush injury to his right forearm. He reports severe worsening pain not relieved by analgesics. On examination, the forearm is swollen, tense, and shiny. Fasciotomy has been initiated. Capillary refill is <2 seconds. When the examiner attempts passive extension of the patient's fingers, he screams in pain. Which of the following is the most specific clinical finding suggesting compartment syndrome?

options.C: Severe pain with passive extension of the fingers

questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Intraoperative photograph showing a longitudinal volar forearm fasciotomy decompression with muscle bellies bulging through the skin and fascial incisions.

Severe pain with passive stretch of the muscles in the affected compartment (e.g., passive extension of the fingers stretching the flexor compartment) is the most sensitive and earliest reliable clinical finding of acute compartment syndrome. Intracompartmental pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure (ΔP = diastolic BP - compartment pressure < 30 mmHg), resulting in muscle ischemia that is intensely provoked by stretching the ischemic muscle fibers.

High-yield takeaway: The 6 Ps of Compartment Syndrome: Pain out of proportion, Pain on passive stretch (earliest/most sensitive), Pressure (tense/woody), Paresthesia, Pallor, Pulselessness (late/irreversible).

Exam trap: Never wait for pulselessness or pallor to diagnose compartment syndrome; by the time pulses disappear, irreversible myonecrosis and nerve infarction have already occurred.

optionExplanations.A: Pulses and capillary refill remain completely normal until very late stages of compartment syndrome, because systemic arterial pressure is significantly higher than intracompartmental capillary closing pressure. The presence of palpable pulses NEVER rules out compartment syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: Compartment syndrome pain is notoriously unyielding and out of proportion, worsening despite immobilization and high-dose narcotics.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Severe pain with passive stretch of the muscles in the affected compartment (e.g., passive extension of the fingers stretching the flexor compartment) is the most sensitive and earliest reliable clinical finding of acute compartment syndrome.
optionExplanations.D: Pulses and capillary refill remain completely normal until very late stages of compartment syndrome, because systemic arterial pressure is significantly higher than intracompartmental capillary closing pressure. The presence of palpable pulses NEVER rules out compartment syndrome.
optionExplanations.E: Paresthesia indicates ischemic nerve compromise and is an important early sign, but passive stretch pain is the hallmark physical exam finding.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize excruciating pain elicited by passive muscular stretch as the most sensitive early clinical indicator of acute compartment syndrome.

questions.question: A patient present with severe leg pain for several hours after casting. Examination shows tense calf muscles, reduced pulse, and paresthesia of the toes. The ATLS steps have been taken into account. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
This patient exhibits advanced acute compartment syndrome following cast application, demonstrated by tense calf compartments, diminished distal pulses, and paresthesias. With ATLS protocols fulfilled, emergent surgical decompression via fasciotomy (in the lower leg: two-incision four-compartment fasciotomy) is the definitive, limb-saving treatment of choice. Note: While external constrictive dressings or casts should immediately be split/removed at the bedside, persistent ischemia and neurological compromise mandate urgent fasciotomy.

High-yield takeaway: In acute compartment syndrome, keep the limb AT HEART LEVEL. Elevating the limb reduces arterial inflow, and placing it dependent worsens edema and venous congestion.

Exam trap: Elevating an extremity with compartment syndrome is a catastrophic board trap that rapidly accelerates ischemic muscle necrosis.

optionExplanations.A: Leg elevation is strictly contraindicated in compartment syndrome because it further decreases arterial perfusion pressure across the high-pressure compartment.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Tense calf, reduced pulse and paresthesia after casting indicate advanced acute compartment syndrome; once the ATLS steps are done, emergent fasciotomy is the definitive treatment.
optionExplanations.C: Advanced imaging like MRI causes fatal delays in tissue decompression and is never indicated when compartment syndrome is clinically apparent.
optionExplanations.D: Observation and analgesia alone without surgical release will lead to ischemic Volkmann contracture, rhabdomyolysis, and limb loss.
optionExplanations.E: Observation and analgesia alone without surgical release will lead to ischemic Volkmann contracture, rhabdomyolysis, and limb loss.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify urgent surgical fasciotomy as the mandatory definitive treatment for acute lower extremity compartment syndrome.

questions.question: A patient came with a swollen, painful, and pulseless fractured hand under a cast. What is the next step in management?

options.B: Remove cast and reassess after 6 hours

questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Clinical photograph of an immobilized hand and forearm in a plaster cast with severely swollen, dusky, cyanotic exposed fingertips, demonstrating distal neurovascular compromise.

A swollen, intensely painful, and pulseless hand under a cast represents advanced acute compartment syndrome of the intrinsic hand muscles (and potentially forearm flexor/extensor compartments) with impending ischemic necrosis. The immediate definitive intervention is urgent operative fasciotomy to decompress the interosseous compartments, thenar, hypothenar, and carpal tunnel spaces. Bedside cast bivalving is done immediately, but waiting 6 hours to reassess would cause irreversible Volkmann ischemic contracture.

High-yield takeaway: Hand compartment syndrome involves 10 separate osteofascial compartments (4 dorsal interossei, 3 volar interossei, thenar, hypothenar, and adductor pollicis), requiring urgent multi-compartment fasciotomy.

Exam trap: Never delay surgical intervention for advanced ischemic symptoms in a casted extremity; irreversible nerve injury begins at 2-4 hours, and muscle necrosis is permanent after 6-8 hours.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A swollen, painful, pulseless hand under a cast is advanced compartment syndrome with impending ischemic necrosis, so urgent fasciotomy is the definitive intervention.
optionExplanations.B: Waiting 6 hours after cast removal is unacceptable; irreversible muscle and nerve necrosis occurs within 4-6 hours of complete ischemia.
optionExplanations.C: Analgesia masks worsening ischemia, and MRI causes unnecessary diagnostic delay in a surgical emergency.
optionExplanations.D: Analgesia masks worsening ischemia, and MRI causes unnecessary diagnostic delay in a surgical emergency.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that acute hand compartment syndrome with neurovascular impairment demands emergent surgical fasciotomy decompression.

questions.question: A patient undergoing surgery for a fracture received cefazolin. Shortly after, the anesthesiologist noticed a sudden onset of bronchospasm, erythematous rash, and dyspnea. What type of shock did this patient most likely develop?
questions.explanation:
The sudden intraoperative onset of bronchospasm, diffuse erythematous cutaneous flush/urticaria, and respiratory distress immediately following administration of cefazolin is diagnostic of anaphylactic shock (Type I hypersensitivity). Cephalosporins (and penicillins) are classic triggers of IgE-mediated histamine and leukotriene release, causing systemic vasodilation (distributive shock), capillary leakage, and bronchoconstriction. Immediate management consists of stopping the offending agent, administering intramuscular or IV epinephrine, aggressive fluid resuscitation, and airway stabilization.

High-yield takeaway: First-line treatment for perioperative anaphylactic shock is EPINEPHRINE (administered immediately). Epinephrine provides alpha-1 vasoconstriction to restore perfusion pressure and beta-2 bronchodilation to relieve bronchospasm.

Exam trap: Antihistamines and corticosteroids are secondary adjunctive therapies; they must NEVER delay the immediate administration of epinephrine in anaphylactic shock.

optionExplanations.A: Septic shock presents with hyperthermia/hypothermia, progressive organ failure, and elevated inflammatory markers over hours to days rather than hyperacute bronchospasm upon antibiotic infusion.
optionExplanations.B: Neurogenic shock results from disruption of sympathetic autonomic pathways following cervical or high thoracic spinal cord injury, presenting with hypotension and bradycardia without bronchospasm or urticaria.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The sudden intraoperative onset of bronchospasm, diffuse erythematous cutaneous flush/urticaria, and respiratory distress immediately following administration of cefazolin is diagnostic of anaphylactic shock (Type I hypersensitivity).

questions.educationalObjective: Identify acute bronchospasm, urticaria, and hemodynamic collapse following perioperative antibiotic infusion as anaphylactic shock.

questions.question: A 46-year-old female came to the ER after a high-energy accident. X-ray shows a fracture in the femur shaft, and the patient was stabilized. After 8 hours, she suddenly started to complain of dyspnea and petechiae. According to this case, what is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Photographs illustrating subconjunctival petechial hemorrhages in both eyes and a classic non-palpable petechial rash across the anterior chest and axillary folds.

The development of acute dyspnea, hypoxemia, and a petechial rash (particularly involving the conjunctiva, axillae, or anterior chest) in a patient with a long bone fracture (femoral shaft) is virtually pathognomonic for Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES). FES occurs when bone marrow fat droplets enter the venous sinusoids at the fracture site and occlude pulmonary microvessels, where lipases break them down into toxic free fatty acids, inducing chemical pneumonitis, diffuse alveolar damage, and microvascular petechiae.

High-yield takeaway: Gurd and Wilson's Criteria for FES: Major features include respiratory distress (hypoxemia PaO2 < 60 mmHg), cerebral involvement (confusion/ drowsiness), and petechial rash. Petechiae appear in ~50% of cases and confirm the diagnosis.

Exam trap: Thromboembolic PE does not cause a petechial rash. The presence of petechiae on the conjunctiva, neck, or axillae in a femur fracture patient is the board giveaway for Fat Embolism Syndrome.

optionExplanations.A: Thromboembolic pulmonary embolism causes sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain but is NOT associated with the characteristic axillary/conjunctival petechial rash seen in FES.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The development of acute dyspnea, hypoxemia, and a petechial rash (particularly involving the conjunctiva, axillae, or anterior chest) in a patient with a long bone fracture (femoral shaft) is virtually pathognomonic for Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES).
optionExplanations.C: Anaphylactic shock presents with immediate urticaria, wheezing, and cardiovascular collapse after drug administration, not isolated petechiae hours after trauma.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the combination of post-traumatic femur fracture, sudden dyspnea, and petechiae as pathognomonic for Fat Embolism Syndrome.

questions.question: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with a pelvic injury and an open fracture of the left femur. What is the best initial management?

options.A: He has an estimated blood loss of 500 mL

questions.explanation:
According to Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) principles, the evaluation and resuscitation of every trauma patient must strictly follow the primary survey sequence: A - Airway maintenance with cervical spine protection; B - Breathing and ventilation; C - Circulation with hemorrhage control; D - Disability (neurological evaluation); E - Exposure and environmental control. Regardless of severe orthopedic injuries (pelvic fracture, open femur fracture), securing a patent airway with in-line cervical stabilization is always the paramount first step.

High-yield takeaway: ATLS Hierarchy: Airway (A) > Breathing (B) > Circulation (C) > Disability (D) > Exposure (E). Never jump to fracture reduction or hemorrhage assessment until airway patency and respiratory ventilation are established.

Exam trap: Dramatic extremity injuries (open femur, mangled limb) frequently distract junior clinicians from the ABCDE sequence. Always secure the airway first.

optionExplanations.A: A pelvic fracture combined with a femur fracture can easily cause massive, life-threatening retroperitoneal and thigh hemorrhage exceeding 2000-3000 mL, far greater than 500 mL. However, addressing airway remains the first step.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. According to Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) principles, the evaluation and resuscitation of every trauma patient must strictly follow the primary survey sequence: A - Airway maintenance with cervical spine protection; B - Breathing and ventilation; C - Circulation with hemorrhage control; D - Disability (neurological evaluation); E - Exposure and environmental control.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply the ATLS primary survey algorithm to ensure that establishing a patent airway precedes all circulatory and orthopedic interventions in polytrauma.

questions.question: What is the PRIMARY indication for applying a pelvic sling?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Clinical demonstration photograph showing healthcare providers applying a commercial pelvic stabilization device (Arrow T-POD pelvic binder) centered over the greater trochanters of a supine trauma patient.

A pelvic sling (or circumferential pelvic binder) is applied during the 'Circulation' (C) phase of the ATLS primary survey. In open-book pelvic fractures (anterior-posterior compression) or vertical shear disruptions, the volume of the true pelvis expands dramatically, leading to exsanguinating hemorrhage from the presacral venous plexus and internal iliac arterial branches into the retroperitoneum. Applying a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters closes the pelvic ring, reduces pelvic volume, promotes a tamponade effect, and stabilizes bone edges to halt massive life-threatening hemorrhage.

High-yield takeaway: Pelvic binders must be centered over the GREATER TROCHANTERS (not the iliac crests) to provide effective mechanical closure of disrupted sacroiliac and pubic symphysis joints and control venous bleeding.

Exam trap: Placing the binder high over the iliac crests does not compress the pelvic ring and can actually worsen fracture displacement and retroperitoneal bleeding.

optionExplanations.A: Airway and Breathing address oxygenation and pulmonary mechanics, not pelvic retroperitoneal vascular hemorrhage.
optionExplanations.B: Airway and Breathing address oxygenation and pulmonary mechanics, not pelvic retroperitoneal vascular hemorrhage.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A pelvic sling (or circumferential pelvic binder) is applied during the 'Circulation' (C) phase of the ATLS primary survey.
optionExplanations.D: Disability assesses neurological status (GCS, pupils), and Exposure involves undressing and hypothermia prevention.
optionExplanations.E: Disability assesses neurological status (GCS, pupils), and Exposure involves undressing and hypothermia prevention.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that pelvic binder placement is an emergency Circulation (C) intervention designed to control pelvic ring hemorrhage through volumetric reduction.

questions.question: A patient with electrical injury and pain in his shoulder. AP X-ray of his shoulder shows specific findings. Which of the following is incorrect about the mechanism of injury?

options.C: It is due to abduction and external rotation

questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Anterior-posterior (AP) radiograph of the right shoulder demonstrating the classic 'lightbulb sign' (fixed internal rotation of the humeral head) and vacant glenoid cavity indicative of posterior glenohumeral dislocation.

Posterior shoulder dislocations are typically caused by violent muscle contractions during electrical shock injuries or epileptic seizures, or by high-energy trauma with an axial load applied to an ADDUCTED, INTERNALLY ROTATED, and FLEXED arm. The internal rotators (latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, subscapularis) overpower the external rotators, driving the humeral head posteriorly. In contrast, abduction and external rotation is the classic mechanism for ANTERIOR shoulder dislocation. Therefore, statement C is INCORRECT regarding posterior dislocation.

High-yield takeaway: Mechanisms of Shoulder Dislocation: Anterior (95%) = Abduction + External Rotation. Posterior (2-4%) = Adduction + Internal Rotation (classic in SEIZURES and ELECTROCUTION).

Exam trap: Up to 50% of posterior shoulder dislocations are missed on initial standard AP radiographs because the humeral head may appear deceptively aligned. An axillary lateral or scapular Y-view is essential.

optionExplanations.A: The provided radiograph demonstrates the right shoulder (anatomical landmarks confirm the right clavicle and humerus).
optionExplanations.B: Electrical injury is a classic cause of posterior shoulder dislocation, producing the lightbulb sign on AP radiograph due to fixed internal rotation.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. This is the incorrect statement: posterior dislocation (lightbulb sign) follows electric shock or seizure muscle contraction, or an axial load on an adducted, internally rotated, flexed arm - not abduction and external rotation.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that posterior shoulder dislocations occur via adduction and internal rotation (frequently following seizures or electrical shock) rather than abduction and external rotation.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman presents with gradual onset of knee pain over 3 years. She reports morning stiffness lasting 15-20 minutes and worsening pain with walking or climbing stairs. On examination, there is mild swelling, crepitus, and reduced range of motion. No history of trauma or systemic inflammatory disease. Based on the clinical presentation and X-ray findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Weight-bearing bilateral knee radiographs showing asymmetric medial compartment joint space narrowing, dense subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cyst formation, and marginal osteophytes (highlighted with yellow circle).

The clinical presentation (age > 50, gradual progression over years, pain exacerbated by weight-bearing/stairs, short morning stiffness < 30 minutes, crepitus, reduced range of motion) together with the radiographic triad of joint space narrowing (typically medial compartment), subchondral sclerosis, osteophytosis, and subchondral cysts is diagnostic of Degenerative Arthritis (Knee Osteoarthritis).

High-yield takeaway: Four Radiographic Hallmarks of Osteoarthritis (LOSS): L - Loss of joint space (asymmetric), O - Osteophytes (bone spurs), S - Subchondral sclerosis (bone whitening), S - Subchondral cysts.

Exam trap: Morning stiffness duration distinguishes osteoarthritis (<30 minutes, worsens with use) from inflammatory arthritis like RA (>60 minutes, improves with activity).

optionExplanations.A: Rheumatoid arthritis features prolonged morning stiffness (> 60 minutes), symmetric tricompartmental narrowing without prominent osteophytes, marginal erosions, and systemic inflammatory signs.
optionExplanations.B: Septic arthritis presents acutely with severe pain, fever, erythema, inability to bear weight, and high synovial leukocyte counts.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Age >50, gradual onset, short morning stiffness (<30 min), crepitus and the radiographic changes (medial joint-space narrowing, sclerosis, cysts, osteophytes) are classic for osteoarthritis.
optionExplanations.D: Gouty arthritis presents with acute, intensely painful monoarticular attacks often involving the first MTP joint or knee, with negative birefringent needle-shaped crystals.
optionExplanations.E: Traumatic meniscal tears usually have an acute twisting injury with mechanical catching, locking, and joint line tenderness.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose primary knee osteoarthritis based on mechanical pain, brief morning stiffness (<30 minutes), crepitus, and classic radiographic signs (osteophytes, asymmetric joint space narrowing).

questions.question: All of the following can cause secondary osteoarthritis except:
questions.explanation:
Secondary osteoarthritis results from an underlying intra-articular insult that alters joint biomechanics, congruence, or articular cartilage viability. Intra-articular fractures (femoral intercondylar fracture, tibial plateau fracture) cause articular step-off and incongruity; previous septic arthritis releases chondrolytic bacterial enzymes causing cartilage destruction; and chronic ACL deficiency causes anteroposterior instability and repetitive shear stress leading to meniscal tears and secondary osteoarthritis of the knee. In contrast, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is an avascular necrosis of the femoral head in the HIP; while it can cause referred pain to the knee via the obturator nerve, it does NOT cause primary structural cartilage pathology or secondary osteoarthritis in the knee joint itself.

High-yield takeaway: Perthes disease causes secondary osteoarthritis of the HIP in adult life, but its referred knee pain does not cause structural osteoarthritis of the knee joint.

Exam trap: Referred pain must never be confused with intrinsic joint pathology. Hip disease in children frequently presents solely as knee pain (via the obturator and femoral nerves), but the knee joint remains structurally pristine.

optionExplanations.A: Intra-articular fractures of the distal femur or tibial plateau directly compromise the articular surface and are prime causes of post-traumatic secondary knee OA.
optionExplanations.B: Septic arthritis destroys proteoglycan matrices and chondrocytes, leading to rapid secondary osteoarthritis.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Perthes disease is avascular necrosis of the femoral head (hip) that only refers pain to the knee; it does not cause knee osteoarthritis, so it is the exception.
optionExplanations.D: Chronic ACL rupture alters translational kinematics, accelerating secondary degenerative change.
optionExplanations.E: Intra-articular fractures of the distal femur or tibial plateau directly compromise the articular surface and are prime causes of post-traumatic secondary knee OA.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate intrinsic articular etiologies of secondary knee osteoarthritis from referred pain originating from proximal hip disease (Perthes).

questions.question: Which of the following statements is CORRECT ?

options.A: Active arthritis affecting the proximal interphalangeal joints of middle and index fingers
options.B: Boutonniere deformity is present in all fingers
options.C: Swan neck deformity affecting all digits

questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Clinical photograph of a patient's hand demonstrating prominent fusiform soft tissue swelling and synovitis centered over the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of the index and middle fingers, without fixed contractures.

The clinical photograph clearly displays fusiform swelling, erythema, and synovial proliferation localized specifically over the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of the 2nd (index) and 3rd (middle) digits. This is characteristic of active inflammatory synovitis / arthritis (e.g., early rheumatoid arthritis or seronegative spondyloarthropathy). Fixed deformities such as boutonnière (PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension) or swan neck (PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion) have not yet developed across all digits.

High-yield takeaway: Symmetric, inflammatory synovitis of the PIP and MCP joints with sparing of the DIP joints is a hallmark of Rheumatoid Arthritis. Fusiform swelling around the PIP joints reflects synovial hypertrophy.

Exam trap: Distinguish between Bouchard nodes (firm, bony osteophytes in osteoarthritis) and spindle-shaped, soft synovial boggy swelling of active rheumatoid synovitis.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The clinical photograph clearly displays fusiform swelling, erythema, and synovial proliferation localized specifically over the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of the 2nd (index) and 3rd (middle) digits.
optionExplanations.B: Boutonnière deformity requires fixed PIP flexion with reciprocal DIP hyperextension, which is absent across all fingers.
optionExplanations.C: Swan neck deformity requires PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion, which is not present in all digits.
optionExplanations.D: [Independently written - the source gives no explanation for this option] This statement may also be factually true: the source image description mentions PIP synovitis and states fixed deformities have not developed, which implies no boutonniere deformity. The source key prefers A as the more complete description. Verify against the original image (possible multiple-correct item).
optionExplanations.E: The index and middle fingers show marked PIP involvement; it is not isolated to the thumb.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize active synovitis affecting the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of the digits in inflammatory arthritis.

questions.question: A 30-year-old patient presents with severe shoulder pain after a tonic-clonic seizure. His arm was adducted and internally rotated. AP X-ray appears below. What is the best next step?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Anterior-posterior (AP) plain radiograph of the shoulder following a seizure, showing loss of normal half-moon glenohumeral overlap, humeral head symmetric circular contour (lightbulb sign), and posterior displacement.

A young patient presenting with severe shoulder pain, an arm held locked in internal rotation and adduction following a tonic-clonic seizure has a posterior shoulder dislocation until proven otherwise. When plain radiographs suggest or fail to conclusively delineate posterior dislocation, computed tomography (CT) of the shoulder is the gold standard next diagnostic step. A CT scan definitively confirms the posterior dislocation, accurately characterizes the size and depth of any anterior humeral head impaction fracture (reverse Hill-Sachs / McLaughlin lesion), and assesses the posterior glenoid rim (reverse Bankart lesion) to guide whether closed reduction or operative reconstruction is safe.

High-yield takeaway: Posterior Shoulder Dislocation Clues: Seizure or electrocution, arm locked in internal rotation (cannot externally rotate), 'Lightbulb sign' on AP radiograph. CT is the best imaging modality to evaluate osseous defects (reverse Hill-Sachs).

Exam trap: Inability to externally rotate the shoulder after a seizure is the key clinical sign of posterior dislocation. Never dismiss an AP view as normal without axillary/Y views or CT.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. An arm locked in adduction and internal rotation after a seizure suggests posterior shoulder dislocation; CT is the next step to confirm it and delineate the bony injury when plain films are inconclusive.
optionExplanations.B: MRI is excellent for soft tissue labral and rotator cuff pathology, but non-contrast CT is far faster, superior for characterizing bony impaction defect size (McLaughlin lesion), and the preferred imaging modality prior to reduction.
optionExplanations.C: Attempting blind closed reduction without determining the size of an impaction defect can cause humeral head collapse or iatrogenic surgical neck fracture if the head is locked onto the posterior glenoid rim.
optionExplanations.D: Open reduction is reserved for chronic, locked, or large impaction defects (>40% articular surface involvement); imaging confirmation with CT must precede surgical decisions.

questions.educationalObjective: Select CT imaging as the best next step to confirm posterior shoulder dislocation and quantify reverse Hill-Sachs impaction defects following epileptic seizures.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the knee joint?

options.A: ACL, PCL, LCL, and MCL are all intra-articular ligaments.
options.B: Modified hinge joint with movement in the sagittal plane and slight transverse movement.

questions.explanation:
The tibiofemoral knee joint is classified structurally as a synovial bicondylar joint, and functionally as a modified hinge (ginglymus) joint. Its primary motion occurs in the sagittal plane (flexion and extension), but it also permits an essential small degree of rotational movement (axial/transverse plane rotation), particularly the 'screw-home mechanism' where the tibia externally rotates during terminal extension to lock the knee joint in stability.

High-yield takeaway: The knee is NOT a simple hinge joint; it is a modified hinge joint because the unequal sizes of the femoral condyles require obligatory internal/ external axial rotation (the screw-home mechanism) during flexion and extension.

Exam trap: MCL and LCL are extra-articular collateral ligaments. Only the ACL and PCL reside inside the fibrous joint capsule.

optionExplanations.A: The ACL and PCL are intra-articular (though extra-synovial) cruciate ligaments, whereas the Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL) and Lateral Collateral Ligament (LCL) are extracapsular/capsular, extra-articular collateral ligaments.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The knee is a modified hinge (bicondylar synovial) joint with mainly sagittal-plane flexion-extension plus a small amount of rotation.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the knee as a modified hinge joint allowing sagittal flexion/extension with coupled axial transverse rotation.

questions.question: The X-ray shows a fracture involving the distal radius in a child, characterized by an incomplete cortical break. What is the most appropriate initial management for this type of injury?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Forearm radiographs of a child showing an incomplete greenstick fracture of the distal radius with plastic deformation: the tension cortex is disrupted while the compression cortex remains in continuity.

Incomplete pediatric fractures with thick, elastic periosteum—such as buckle (torus) or stable non-displaced greenstick fractures of the distal radius—have tremendous remodeling potential and excellent intrinsic stability. The standard of care is non-operative management with cast immobilization (a short arm or sugar-tong/long arm cast depending on stability) for 3 to 4 weeks. Invasive surgery like ORIF or percutaneous K-wiring is entirely unnecessary and contraindicated for simple incomplete fractures.

High-yield takeaway: Pediatric greenstick and torus fractures heal rapidly within 3-4 weeks with simple cast immobilization due to thick, vascular periosteum and high osteogenic potential.

Exam trap: Never subject a stable pediatric greenstick or buckle fracture to unnecessary surgical hardware.

optionExplanations.A: Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) risks iatrogenic physeal damage, infection, and periosteal devascularization in a pediatric patient with an easily treatable incomplete fracture.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Incomplete (buckle/greenstick) distal radius fractures in children are stable and remodel well, so non-operative treatment in a short arm cast is standard.
optionExplanations.C: Percutaneous K-wire fixation is reserved for unstable, displaced supracondylar humerus or completely displaced distal radius physeal fractures that fail closed reduction.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify below-elbow (short arm) cast immobilization as the treatment of choice for incomplete distal radius fractures in children.

questions.question: Examine the following forearm X-ray. Which of the following best describes the fracture?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): AP and lateral forearm radiographs demonstrating an incomplete transverse fracture line involving only one cortex of the radial diaphysis with intact opposing cortex (classic greenstick fracture).

The radiograph demonstrates a classic incomplete (greenstick) fracture of the radius. In children, bone has a lower mineral content and higher collagen matrix elasticity, allowing bones to bend plastically before failing. In a greenstick fracture, the cortex on the tension (convex) side breaks, while the cortex on the compression (concave) side remains in continuity without complete separation.

High-yield takeaway: Greenstick fracture: incomplete fracture unique to pediatric long bones where one cortex is fractured and the opposing cortex is plastically deformed/buckled.

Exam trap: Ensure completion of reduction if a greenstick fracture has significant angulation; sometimes the intact cortex must be gently completed during reduction to prevent recurrence of deformity.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The radiograph demonstrates a classic incomplete (greenstick) fracture of the radius. In children, bone has a lower mineral content and higher collagen matrix elasticity, allowing bones to bend plastically before failing.
optionExplanations.B: The fracture demonstrates coronal/incomplete unicortical disruption rather than primarily posterior apex angulation.

questions.educationalObjective: Correctly identify an incomplete (greenstick) fracture pattern on pediatric forearm radiographs.

questions.question: An adult patient came to the ER complaining of pain after falling down. X-ray shows a femur fracture. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Radiograph of an adult femur showing a completely displaced midshaft (diaphyseal) femoral fracture with substantial shortening and soft tissue swelling.

In adults, diaphyseal femoral shaft fractures are high-energy injuries that require surgical stabilization. The gold standard treatment is reamed antegrade (or retrograde) intramedullary nailing (IMN). Intramedullary nailing functions as a load-sharing internal splint that allows early mobilization, promotes secondary bone healing through micromotion and abundant periosteal callus formation, achieves union rates >95%, and minimizes complication rates.

High-yield takeaway: Reamed intramedullary nailing is the definitive standard of care for adult femoral shaft fractures, providing high union rates and allowing rapid weight-bearing.

Exam trap: Do not treat adult femur fractures conservatively with traction or casting; this historical practice carries unacceptable rates of nonunion, malunion, and DVT/pulmonary complications.

optionExplanations.A: Closed reduction and casting (hip spica) in adults is ineffective due to massive deforming muscle forces (iliopsoas, gluteals, adductors, quadriceps) causing severe shortening, malunion, and prolonged bed rest complications.
optionExplanations.B: External fixation is reserved for damage control orthopedics in unstable polytrauma or severe Gustilo IIIB/C open fractures with extensive soft tissue contamination.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Adult femoral shaft fractures are high-energy injuries treated surgically; reamed intramedullary nailing is the gold standard, acting as a load-sharing internal splint that allows early mobilization.
optionExplanations.D: Closed reduction and casting (hip spica) in adults is ineffective due to massive deforming muscle forces (iliopsoas, gluteals, adductors, quadriceps) causing severe shortening, malunion, and prolonged bed rest complications.

questions.educationalObjective: Select reamed intramedullary nailing as the optimal definitive treatment for closed adult femoral shaft fractures.

questions.question: The structure pointed by the arrow represents which phase of fracture healing?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Follow-up radiograph of a healing long bone fracture demonstrating prominent fusiform soft-to-hard callus bridging the fracture gap (indicated by yellow arrow), characteristic of the reparative phase.

Secondary (indirect) bone healing occurs in four overlapping phases: 1) Inflammatory phase (hematoma formation, cytokine release, days 1-5); 2) Reparative phase (soft cartilaginous callus formed by chondrocytes, followed by endochondral ossification into hard woven bone callus, weeks 2-8); 3) Remodeling phase (woven bone replaced by organized lamellar bone along lines of stress per Wolff's law, months to years). The robust periosteal callus pointed by the arrow represents the REPAIR (reparative) phase.

High-yield takeaway: Fracture Callus Stages: Soft callus (cartilage) -> Hard callus (woven bone) during the REPAIR phase. Endochondral ossification transforms soft callus into rigid hard callus.

Exam trap: Callus formation is the hallmark of secondary (indirect) bone healing with relative stability (casts, IM nails). Absolute rigid stability (compression plating) leads to primary direct healing WITHOUT visible callus.

optionExplanations.A: [Independently written - the source gives no explanation for this option] "Mechanical phase" is not one of the standard biological phases of secondary fracture healing (inflammatory, reparative, remodeling). The radiograph shows callus formation, i.e., the repair phase.
optionExplanations.B: [Independently written - the source gives no explanation for this option] "Vascular phase" is not a standard named phase in the inflammatory-reparative-remodeling model used in the source; the visible callus bridging the gap corresponds to the repair phase.
optionExplanations.C: The inflammatory phase occurs immediately within the first 1-2 weeks and consists of hematoma without radiographically visible bony callus.
optionExplanations.D: The remodeling phase occurs over months to years after clinical union, during which medullary canal continuity is restored and excess external callus is resorbed.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The callus bridging the fracture gap corresponds to the repair (reparative) phase of secondary bone healing, which follows the inflammatory phase and precedes remodeling.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that radiographic external bridging callus represents the reparative phase of secondary fracture healing.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about this fracture X-ray?

options.B: Angulation with the apex pointing lateral

questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): AP plain radiograph of the lower leg showing an oblique mid-diaphyseal tibial fracture. The distal bone fragment is translated laterally relative to the proximal shaft with clear displacement between cortical margins.

Evaluating fracture alignment requires describing four key spatial parameters: 1) Translation/displacement (shift of the distal fragment relative to proximal); 2) Angulation (direction of the apex of deformity); 3) Shortening/distraction (loss or gain of longitudinal length); and 4) Rotation. In this radiograph, the predominant feature is significant cortical displacement (translation) across the fracture line.

High-yield takeaway: Displacement is described by the percentage of cortical contact or millimeters of translation of the DISTAL fragment relative to the PROXIMAL fragment.

Exam trap: Always describe fracture displacement and angulation from the perspective of the distal fragment relative to the anatomical proximal shaft.

optionExplanations.A: [Independently written - the source gives no explanation for this option] Rotational alignment cannot be judged reliably from a single AP radiograph, and the source does not state the rotational status; the source rationale identifies displacement (translation) as the predominant finding.
optionExplanations.B: [Independently written - the source gives no explanation for this option] The source rationale describes translation (displacement) as the predominant feature and reports no angulation with a lateral apex.
optionExplanations.C: The radiograph demonstrates the tibia and fibula of the lower leg marked with 'L' (left), not the forearm.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Evaluating fracture alignment requires describing four key spatial parameters: 1) Translation/displacement (shift of the distal fragment relative to proximal); 2) Angulation (direction of the apex of deformity); 3) Shortening/distraction (loss or gain of longitudinal length); and 4) Rotation.
optionExplanations.E: [Independently written - the source gives no explanation for this option] The source image description states the distal fragment is translated laterally, so this statement appears true and overlaps with option D, which the source key prefers. Possible multiple-correct item.

questions.educationalObjective: Demonstrate systematic orthopedic terminology for describing fracture displacement on plain radiographs.

questions.question: A 75-year-old woman fell at home and is unable to walk. X-ray shows a displaced neck of femur fracture. What is the best management?
questions.explanation:
In an elderly patient (>65-70 years old) with a DISPLACED intracapsular femoral neck fracture (Garden III or IV), the blood supply to the femoral head (predominantly the medial femoral circumflex artery ascending retinacular branches) is disrupted. Attempting ORIF in this demographic carries an unacceptably high rate of avascular necrosis (AVN, up to 30-45%) and nonunion (up to 30%). Therefore, the definitive treatment of choice is hip arthroplasty—specifically hemiarthroplasty (or total hip arthroplasty in active community ambulators without cognitive impairment) to allow immediate post-operative full weight-bearing.

High-yield takeaway: Displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture in elderly (>65) = ARTHROPLASTY (hemiarthroplasty or THA). In young patients (<60) = Urgent emergent anatomical reduction and ORIF to salvage the native head.

Exam trap: Do not confuse intracapsular (femoral neck) fractures with extracapsular (intertrochanteric) fractures. Neck fractures disrupt the blood supply (risk of AVN -> replace), while trochanteric fractures have rich metaphyseal blood supply (heal well -> fix with DHS or cephalomedullary nail).

optionExplanations.A: ORIF (cannulated screws) is reserved for non-displaced (Garden I/II) fractures in the elderly or displaced fractures in young patients (<60) where femoral head preservation is paramount.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. In an elderly patient with a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture the femoral head blood supply is disrupted; hemiarthroplasty avoids the high avascular necrosis and nonunion rate of fixation.
optionExplanations.C: A dynamic hip screw (DHS) is the treatment of choice for stable extracapsular intertrochanteric fractures, not displaced intracapsular femoral neck fractures.
optionExplanations.D: Casting cannot stabilize a displaced femoral neck fracture and causes fatal recumbency complications (pneumonia, decubitus ulcers, DVT).

questions.educationalObjective: Select hemiarthroplasty as the optimal surgical treatment for displaced femoral neck fractures in elderly patients to prevent AVN and nonunion.

questions.question: A 70-year-old patient underwent hemiarthroplasty surgery. Which of the following is true?

options.A: He can bear full weight immediately
options.C: The patient will start physiotherapy in two weeks

questions.explanation:
The primary clinical objective of performing hip hemiarthroplasty (cemented or uncemented stem) for hip fractures in elderly patients is to achieve immediate prosthetic stability that allows immediate full weight-bearing on post-operative day 1. Early ambulation and physiotherapy minimize the catastrophic morbidity and mortality associated with prolonged bed rest, such as atelectasis, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and sarcopenia.

High-yield takeaway: Hemiarthroplasty enables immediate full weight-bearing mobilization within 24 hours of surgery, drastically reducing 30-day and 1-year mortality in geriatric hip fracture patients.

Exam trap: There is no risk of AVN of the femoral head following hemiarthroplasty because the femoral head has been discarded!

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The primary clinical objective of performing hip hemiarthroplasty (cemented or uncemented stem) for hip fractures in elderly patients is to achieve immediate prosthetic stability that allows immediate full weight-bearing on post-operative day 1.
optionExplanations.B: Avascular necrosis (AVN) is eliminated as a risk factor because the native femoral head has been resected and replaced with a metallic prosthetic head.
optionExplanations.C: Physiotherapy begins immediately on postoperative day 1, not after two weeks of delay.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that immediate full weight-bearing and prompt mobilization on post-operative day 1 are key advantages of hip hemiarthroplasty.

questions.question: A 6-year-old child presents with a suprascapular humerus fracture. Closed reduction was attempted but unsuccessful. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
In a child presenting with a displaced supracondylar humerus fracture (referred to in exam text as suprascapular/supracondylar), the standard management is closed reduction and percutaneous pinning (CRPP) with Kirschner wires (K-wires). However, when closed reduction fails (typically due to interposition of the brachialis muscle, median nerve, or brachial artery), the mandatory next step is OPEN reduction through an anterior or posterior approach to extract entrapped soft tissues, achieve anatomical reduction, and stabilize with cross or lateral divergent K-wires.

High-yield takeaway: Failed closed reduction of a displaced supracondylar fracture in a child indicates soft tissue interposition (brachialis muscle, brachial artery, or median nerve) and requires OPEN reduction and internal fixation with K-wires.

Exam trap: Never hyperflex an elbow in a cast to maintain reduction if distal pulses weaken; this triggers forearm acute compartment syndrome (Volkmann contracture).

optionExplanations.A: Placing an unreduced, displaced supracondylar fracture in a long arm cast leads to malunion (cubitus varus / gunstock deformity) and severely increases the risk of Volkmann ischemic contracture from compartment compression.
optionExplanations.B: Skeletal traction (Dunlop traction) is obsolete in modern pediatric trauma centers when surgical stabilization is readily available.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. In a child presenting with a displaced supracondylar humerus fracture (referred to in exam text as suprascapular/supracondylar), the standard management is closed reduction and percutaneous pinning (CRPP) with Kirschner wires (K-wires).
optionExplanations.D: Observation of a displaced supracondylar humerus fracture guarantees devastating functional loss, neurovascular compromise, and severe deformity.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify open reduction and K-wire fixation as the correct management for pediatric supracondylar humerus fractures that cannot be reduced by closed maneuvers.

questions.question: A 9-year-old child presents after falling on an outstretched hand. X-ray of the forearm shows a fracture of both the radius and ulna with clear angular displacement. Which of the following BEST describes the deformity seen in this injury?
questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): AP radiograph of a pediatric forearm demonstrating a midshaft fracture of both radius and ulna with lateral translation and deviation of the distal segment.

On the coronal (AP) projection of this forearm radiograph, the distal forearm fragments (radius and ulna) are shifted and angled laterally (toward the radial side), which is described as lateral deviation (radial deviation).

High-yield takeaway: In both-bone forearm fractures, restoring the radial bow and preventing rotational/angular malalignment is vital to preserve pronation and supination.

Exam trap: Remember that AP radiographs evaluate coronal plane alignment (lateral/medial deviation), while lateral radiographs evaluate sagittal plane alignment (volar/dorsal apex angulation).

optionExplanations.A: Correct. On the coronal (AP) projection of this forearm radiograph, the distal forearm fragments (radius and ulna) are shifted and angled laterally (toward the radial side), which is described as lateral deviation (radial deviation).
optionExplanations.B: Medial deviation (ulnar deviation) shifts the distal segment toward the medial/ulnar side, opposite of what is seen on the image.
optionExplanations.C: Apex dorsal and apex volar angulations are sagittal plane deformities best visualized and characterized on a lateral radiograph.
optionExplanations.D: Apex dorsal and apex volar angulations are sagittal plane deformities best visualized and characterized on a lateral radiograph.

questions.educationalObjective: Accurately characterize coronal plane fracture displacement as lateral (radial) deviation on forearm radiographs.

questions.question: A fracture that has not healed and will not heal is called:
questions.explanation:
A nonunion is defined clinically and radiographically as a fracture that has failed to heal within an expected timeframe (traditionally >6-9 months) and shows no progressive signs of healing over 3 consecutive months, such that surgical intervention is mandatory to achieve bony union. By definition, a nonunion has arrested healing and will NOT heal without surgical intervention (debridement, biological stimulation with bone grafting, and rigid mechanical stabilization).

High-yield takeaway: Classification of Nonunion: 1) Hypertrophic nonunion ('elephant foot') = adequate biology/vascularity, inadequate mechanical stability (treat with rigid fixation); 2) Atrophic nonunion = poor biology/avascularity, absent callus (treat with debridement, bone graft, and rigid fixation).

Exam trap: Do not confuse delayed union (slow healing, will eventually unite) with nonunion (healing has ceased, will NEVER unite without intervention).

optionExplanations.A: Malunion refers to a fracture that HAS healed, but in an unacceptable anatomical position (angular, rotational, or short alignment).
optionExplanations.B: Delayed union refers to a fracture that is taking longer than the anticipated normal timeframe to heal, but still maintains biological activity and healing potential to eventually unite without surgery.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A nonunion is defined clinically and radiographically as a fracture that has failed to heal within an expected timeframe (traditionally >6-9 months) and shows no progressive signs of healing over 3 consecutive months, such that surgical intervention is mandatory to achieve bony union.

questions.educationalObjective: Define fracture nonunion as a complete arrest of the repair process where bony union will not occur without active surgical intervention.

questions.question: The axon remains intact, and there is no axonal degeneration; the nerve is structurally preserved. This refers to:
questions.explanation:
Under the Seddon and Sunderland classifications of peripheral nerve injury: 1) Neuropraxia (Grade I): Focal demyelination or physiologic conduction block without axonal disruption; the axon remains intact, no Wallerian degeneration occurs, and full spontaneous recovery typically occurs within weeks to months. 2) Axonotmesis (Grade II-IV): Axonal discontinuity with Wallerian degeneration distal to the injury, but the surrounding connective tissue sheaths (endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium) remain intact or partially intact. 3) Neurotmesis (Grade V): Complete structural severance of both the axon and all supporting connective tissue sheaths, precluding spontaneous recovery without microsurgical repair.

High-yield takeaway: Seddon Nerve Injury Classification: Neuropraxia = conduction block, intact axon, NO Wallerian degeneration (excellent prognosis). Axonotmesis = axon severed, sheath intact, Wallerian degeneration present (regenerates 1 mm/day). Neurotmesis = complete nerve transection (requires surgery).

Exam trap: In neuropraxia, EMG shows absence of denervation potentials (fibrillations and positive sharp waves) because the axon is intact.

optionExplanations.A: In axonotmesis, the axon is disrupted and undergoes Wallerian degeneration distal to the lesion.
optionExplanations.B: In neurotmesis, the entire nerve trunk (axon and surrounding connective tissue stromata) is completely severed.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Under the Seddon and Sunderland classifications of peripheral nerve injury: 1) Neuropraxia (Grade I): Focal demyelination or physiologic conduction block without axonal disruption; the axon remains intact, no Wallerian degeneration occurs, and full spontaneous recovery typically occurs within weeks to months.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize neuropraxia as a physiologic conduction block with structural preservation of the axon and absence of Wallerian degeneration.

questions.question: True about this condition (physeal fracture):

options.A: It is complicated by complete or incomplete growth arrest

questions.explanation:
Clinical/radiographic presentation (source description): Radiograph of the distal tibia showing a vertical fracture extending through the epiphysis, crosses the physis, and traverses the metaphysis (Salter-Harris Type IV fracture).

Physeal (growth plate) injuries, particularly intra-articular fractures crossing the physis (Salter-Harris Type III and Type IV), violate the germinal and proliferating cartilage zones.
